name: ALEKS
line: ALEKS assesses in separate Knowledge Checks. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review happen at every problem.
description: AMP vs ALEKS: ALEKS assesses in Knowledge Checks, then offers topics. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous, at every problem.
verdict: ALEKS assesses in Knowledge Checks, separate from learning, and offers the topics a learner is ready for [1][3]. In AMP, assessment and teaching are continuous. Every answer updates the learner's level and sets the next problem, and each problem carries its own hint, lesson and worked answer.

reasons.title: Continuous assessment
reasons.body: AMP has no separate test. Every answer, right or wrong, updates the learner's level in that part of math and sets the next problem. ALEKS assesses in Knowledge Checks: one to begin, and more through the course, during which new learning pauses [2][4].

reasons.title: The problem is the unit
reasons.body: In AMP, everything a learner needs hangs off the problem in front of them: a hint that gives the first step, a lesson with a worked example, a video lesson, the worked answer afterward, and links to the skills it builds on and leads to. ALEKS offers a topic, with feedback and learning aids beside its problems [3][6]. Across 55 studies, worked examples improve performance in math [16].

reasons.title: Help is recorded, not forbidden
reasons.body: In AMP an answer given after a hint or a lesson is marked as helped and does not count as learned. A skill counts when the learner gets it right without help, more than once. So help stays in reach all the time. ALEKS asks parents not to help during an assessment, which keeps its measurement clean [5].

reasons.title: Continuous review
reasons.body: In AMP, learned skills come back in ordinary practice, at growing intervals, mixed with other math. In ALEKS, review runs through the Knowledge Checks: a topic missed there goes back to be learned again [4]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [15].

reasons.title: A level for each part of math
reasons.body: AMP keeps a separate level for each part of math, from counting to precalculus. A learner further along in geometry than in fractions gets work at both levels, and repeated misses send practice back to what a skill builds on. ALEKS works one course at a time, and moving to another course is a step the adult takes [7][8].

rows.range: Grade 3 through college math, one course at a time [9][7].
rows.start: A separate adaptive test, the Initial Knowledge Check, taken without help [2][5].
rows.teaching: Problems with immediate feedback and learning aids [6].
rows.next: ALEKS offers the topics it finds the learner ready to learn [3].
rows.mastery: Decided by Knowledge Checks. A topic missed there goes back to be learned again [4].
rows.review: Knowledge Checks that return through the course to retest it [4].
rows.adult: Chooses the course, and changes it by hand [8].
rows.evidence: A meta-analysis: as good as classroom teaching, not better [12]. A randomized trial: no significant gain [13].

theirs: ALEKS stands for Assessment and Learning in Knowledge Spaces. It grew from Knowledge Space Theory, research led by Jean-Claude Falmagne at the University of California, Irvine, and it is now part of McGraw Hill [1][11]. The theory maps the states of knowledge a student can be in, and uses an adaptive test to find which one a student is in [2].

A learner takes an Initial Knowledge Check and sees the course as a pie chart [2][10]. ALEKS then offers the topics it finds the learner ready to learn [3], and Knowledge Checks return through the course to retest what was learned [4].
credit: A serious theory of what a learner is ready for, built by researchers over decades [1][2].
It checks whether learning held. A topic that did not stick goes back on the path [4].
It has been studied by people outside the company [12][13].

theirs: The broadest study is a meta-analysis by Fang, Ren, Hu and Graesser (2019) of 15 studies of ALEKS with secondary and college students. It found ALEKS "as good, but not better than, traditional classroom teaching" [12].

The What Works Clearinghouse has reviewed one randomized trial, Craig et al. (2013), which assigned 253 sixth graders to ALEKS or to teacher-led lessons after school. On the state test it found no statistically significant positive findings [13]. Evidence for ESSA lists ALEKS without a rating, because no studies met its inclusion requirements [14].
ours: The two findings AMP leans on hardest: worked examples improve math performance across 55 studies [16], and practice that mixes and spaces topics scored 62% against 38% for practice in blocks a month later, in a randomized trial that meets What Works Clearinghouse standards without reservations [15]. AMP applies both at every problem.

AMP's own outcome studies are planned: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. The research behind each part of AMP is in our report, and AMP is open source.

them: You want a separate test to decide what a learner is ready for, and a retest of the course at intervals.
amp: You want assessment, teaching and review in the same practice, with no separate tests.
You want a hint, a lesson and the worked answer at every problem.
You want learned skills to keep coming back in practice.
Your learner is at different levels in different parts of math.

questions.question: How is AMP different from ALEKS?
questions.answer: ALEKS assesses with Knowledge Checks, then offers the topics a learner is ready for [2][3]. AMP has no separate test: every answer sets the next problem, each problem carries its own teaching, and learned skills return in ordinary practice.

questions.question: Does ALEKS work?
questions.answer: A meta-analysis of 15 studies found ALEKS as good as classroom teaching, not better [12]. The one randomized trial reviewed by the What Works Clearinghouse found no statistically significant gain over teacher-led lessons [13].

questions.question: Can a learner use both?
questions.answer: Yes. They are separate programs. AMP places a learner from their first answers, whatever else they use.
